text:
Goldman’s note this morning says $CRWV can still generate ~15% unlevered IRRs even assuming its GPUs are worth zero after five years with new long-term contracts starting ~$13M/MW versus ~$10M/MW blended today.

They also said the scary 15% unsecured bond yield also overstates the capital stack because Goldman puts CoreWeave’s blended cost of debt closer to 9% with most borrowing secured by GPUs and customer contracts while managed-inference and Omni can lift revenue per MW without requiring equivalent new infrastructure.

The catch is obviously efficiency because Goldman’s model implies a roughly 3-year payback versus closer to two years for $IREN and $NBIS.

text:
I’ve long felt that a $SPCX - $TSLA deal is inevitable since Elon controls 48% of $SPCX as-converted shares and 10.5% of TSLA shares. Since any deal would be $SPCX stock for $TSLA stock the deal will not be as compelling as many on X believe, given the massive dilution and all-equity economics.  I expect a SPCX offer price in the neighborhood of $420/TSLA share, and as in most stock-for-stock deals will likely get arbitraged down given the approximate 6-12 months needed between a deal announcement and deal close.  

I would expect the combined SPCX/TSLA multiple of EBITDA or EPS to follow the acquiring company’s multiple, which in this case is $SPCX and is lower than TSLA’s FY’27 EV/Ebitda multiple (TSLA 72.6x, SPCX 29.4x).  All told, I don’t expect a huge windfall for TSLA shareholders on a SPCX/TSLA stock-for-stock deal, although the announcement itself would be positive for TSLA stock.

"Last week, our Asia team, led by Howard Kao, received significant media attention for cutting its AMD substrate forecast. This appeared to be more of a housekeeping adjustment, albeit a large one, to a number that we have zero ability to triangulate to AMD shipments.

zh_summary: US inflation remains too high and expected to stay that way. Underlying sticky-price inflation (Atlanta Fed) runs at 2.8% versus 3.7% headline, down from 6.7% in late 2022. Tightening financial conditions may give the Fed a way out of additional rate hikes. Expects inflation around 3% as the new normal; a drop to 2.8% would allow the Fed to halt its hiking cycle.
en_summary: US inflation remains too high and expected to stay that way. Underlying sticky-price inflation (Atlanta Fed) runs at 2.8% versus 3.7% headline, down from 6.7% in late 2022. Tightening financial conditions may give the Fed a way out of additional rate hikes. Expects inflation around 3% as the new normal; a drop to 2.8% would allow the Fed to halt its hiking cycle.
text:
US inflation remains too high.

And I expect it to stay that way.

But underlying inflation looks less alarming. According to the Atlanta Fed, sticky-price inflation, which measures prices that change relatively infrequently, runs well below headline inflation: 2.8% versus 3.7%.

In late 2022, "sticky" prices were rising at a 6.7% annual rate.

With financial conditions already tightening since August, this could give the Federal Reserve a way out of several additional rate hikes.

An October rate hike is not really on the table, but it will be interesting to see whether Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who rarely gives much away at FOMC press conferences, acknowledges any of this.

I believe inflation around 3% will become the new normal.

And if headline inflation falls from today's 3.7% to, say, 2.8%, matching sticky-price inflation, I expect both investors and the Fed to celebrate.

Not because inflation has been defeated. But because it would give the Fed a chance to halt its rate-hiking cycle.

At that point, the Fed may be ready to declare victory at 3% inflation and leave markets alone. But your purchasing power won't be celebrating just yet.

en_summary: In the Netherlands, assets over €30,000 considered wealthy with 36% tax on realized investment gains including those compensating for inflation; government requires tracking all transactions. Finance minister proposes taxing directly held crypto and precious metals on unrealized gains, while ETF-like products taxed on realized, applying two systems to same asset. Responding to discussion on wealth tax administrative costs.
text:
Hi @TruthGundlach,  

Here in the Netherlands, anyone with more than €30,000 in assets is considered wealthy.  

They get to pay a 36% tax on realized investment gains, including gains that just compensate for inflation. 

The government expects investors to keep track of every transaction themselves and report everything to the tax authorities.

And to keep things simple, our finance minister has proposed taxing directly held crypto and precious metals on unrealized gains instead. 

Give up direct ownership and buy an ETF-like product? You're back to being taxed on realized gains. 

Yes, the idea is to apply two tax systems to the same underlying asset.

All of this, of course, for the benefit of investors and a tax authority that has been struggling with overwhelming complexity and workloads for years.

Greetings from Rotterdam,  
Jeroen Blokland

en_summary: Precompiles and EVM are the wrong place for most cryptography support in Ethereum because they operate on data that must be included in the chain as calldata, with practical limits around 8 MB/s even with PeerDAS. Ethereum is a cryptographic world computer, so data/computation not needed in the main execution thread should not be placed there. Ideal route for broader cryptography support is through other mechanisms.
text:
Ultimately, precompiles and EVM are both the wrong place to put most cryptography support into Ethereum. The reason is that precompiles and EVM both operate on data that has to be included into the ethereum chain somehow, which realistically means included in a block as calldata. That space is limited - even with PeerDAS and blocks-in-blobs, there's a practical cap of ~8 MB/s before it starts getting uncomfortable.

Remember: it's not a blockchain. It's a cryptographic world computer. Any data/computation that does not need to be in the "main thread" of data/execution should not be put into the main thread.

Instead, the correct solution is... EIP-8288 maximalism.

If you have any heavy computation that's self-contained, compute it and STARK it client-side (this is quickly getting faster and faster, even on phones), and push the STARK through the EIP-8288 recursive aggregation mechanism. The chain sees the fact that the computation was done and what the result is; it never needs to see the actual data and computation.

This way everyone can use whatever cryptography they want, the Ethereum chain can be lean, and we never need to add more precompiles again.

Kraken co-CEO Arjun Sethi calls going public in the US the slowest piece of financial plumbing left

"Going public in the United States is expensive. It is the slowest piece of financial plumbing left."

"I'm living it, and so are my portfolio companies."

"What I've seen up close from the founder side, sitting on the boards of companies and investing in them is time. The process is measured in quarters and years, not weeks."

"Audits, controls, filings, every number defined and then redefined and then restructured. Every metric then is argued over with people who have never run your business in any capacity."

"Frankly, they learn more on your dime than they can give you advice for."

en_summary: Scott Melker (@scottmelker) shares Kraken co-CEO Arjun Sethi saying unlike banks he does not want to pocket the interest margin and wants to give most of that yield back to customers, emphasizing innovation, disrupting own products, and not seeking net interest margin for themselves.
text:
Kraken co-CEO Arjun Sethi says unlike banks, he doesn't want to pocket the interest margin, and wants to give most of that yield back to customers

"As we're moving more into our own rails and infrastructure, we have to innovate and actually disrupt some of our existing products and make it where we make less money or we don't make money."

"When you think about fees or intermediaries or even things that we charge for over time, we have to be able to continue to bring that down or move on with a new business model, because someone else will actually go out and say, I don't want to rent-seek this."

"I think that ends up becoming a really important piece of any of these traditional institutions, which is how are they going to innovate moving forward?"

"The one thing we continue to hear is you need to be able to be a bank to be able to offer yield. Well, I'm not interested in the net interest margin for ourselves."

"In some cases, it'll be good for us. But in many cases, imagine bringing all that interest margin back to our customers. It's their yield."

"I just think that's just such a core piece of what you want to be able to do on behalf of your customers."
